newsitem.title: UK: Raw materials gain value as dollar, bonds and equities ease.
newsitem.headline: Raw materials gain value as dollar, bonds and equities ease.

text.p: World commodity markets generally firmed on Thursday with copper, gold and coffee all advancing as the dollar weakened and bonds and equities eased with it. Traders said some spoeculative money that presumably left other investments sought a home in the commodities, even bouying lacklustre precious metals. But they were wary of forecasting a strong rally. An active day also saw another big jump on world freight rates -- on which an unsung but dramatic turnaround in the last month may have escaped the eye of inflation-wary finance ministers. The flagship industrial metal, copper, rebounded above $2,000 per tonne. A burst of investment bank buying and shortcovering pushed the benchmark three months delivery London Metal Exchange (LME) copper price up to $2,008.
The move represented a near $40 a tonne gain from Wednesday but traders did not see it as particularly significant as the market was still within a recent $1,950 to $2,040 trading range.
"There was no news behind the rise which was mainly influenced by technical factors," said Martin Squires at brokers Rudolf Wolff.

Aluminium also firmed by some $33 to trade above $1,460 on tight supply for January and speculative interest. Benchmark Chicago Board of Trade (CBOT) wheat was up sharply early in fast dealings as Cargill Inc bought one half million bushels, traders said.
The commercial buying caused locals to cover short positions.
Traders said weekly US wheat export data looked good and the market took note of news that the Turkish Grain Board may import 400,000 to 500,000 tonnes to curb rises in bread prices.
December wheat was soon some 7-1/2 cents firmer above $3.75 per bushel.
Grain prices have been declining. Bumper crops this year followed recent drought in several nations that had depressed world food stocks to the lowest in 20 years.
But brokerage GNI Ltd sounded a note of caution this week when its latest Commodity Perspective said grain stocks were still low and "the wheat market is very oversold".
The world benchmark Brent Blend of crude oil was trading around $22.25 per barrel late in London's afternoon, just easier from Wednesday.

But the gold price picked up to a London close at $379.45 per ounce after $379.15 on Wednesday, helped by a weaker dollar and easier bonds and equities. "There's been some short covering. The bond and stock markets are not looking particularly great," one dealer said.
"The trouble is that when investment comes across from the paper markets in to the precious sector, it tends to move right back out again," he added.
The dollar was under 112 yen in Europe at the afternoon gold fix having closed in London on Wednesday at 113.90 yen.

Elsewhere in commodity markets coffee rallied after speculative buying in New York. Producer country selling capped the advance but London January robusta type futures nonetheless ended higher by $45 at $1,456 per tonne. Cocoa eased slightly but sugar steadied after a sharp technical decline.
Freight rates extended a rebound from recent lows. The Baltic Freight Index (BFI) recorded its biggest single daily increase for 18 months, up 40 points to 1,433, a level last seen on May 15th.

The index is compiled by the Baltic Exchange in London based on rates for key charter routes. Brokers said vessels and cargoes are now being turned over and relet, especially by South Korean operators, at bewildering speed.
